newsitem.title: UK: Copper slumps again on LME, ends weak near lows.
newsitem.headline: Copper slumps again on LME, ends weak near lows.

text.p: Copper prices turned sharply lower during late LME Wednesday ring and kerb trading, with the market ending weak and near 4-1/2 month lows.
Traders said a mid-afternoon spell of consolidation in the $2,260s proved to be illusory, when the market buckled under a renewed bout of speculative liquidation.
This took prices conclusively under $2,240/45 support, and established $2,200 as an initial downside objective.
"It does not look good at all...and it tends to get sold off late because you can move it in low volume in New York," one floor trader said.
Analysts said sentiment has become increasingly sour in recent sessions, with metal stocks rising and demand slowing down for summer.

Consumer vacations result in reduced metal unit requirements, while most producers work around the clock. This leads to stockpiles rising, and recent LME warehouse inventory data indicate that a stock uptrend is now in place, they noted.
Traders said copper's sell-off had become increasingly likely, as the stocks increased and expectations of sizeable arrivals to come circulated.
Also, the July tightness, although still evident, was less intense than at the start of the week. The July "third Wednesday" will be traded next Monday.
The benchmark cash/threes backwardation narrowed into $110 on Wednesday, against levels of $150 at the start of the week.
Final three months trade was at $2,236, a hefty $132 down from Tuesday's kerb after the deluge of investment fund sales, long liquidation, and option-related sales of the last 24 hours.
Since mid-June, when copper peaked for the year at $2,609 a tonne, prices have shed some 14 percent, and the decline has further to go, traders said.
Elsewhere, metal prices wobbled, but once an initial mark-down with copper was not translated into similar selling some stabilised.
Aluminium climbed away from a potential test of sell-stops near $1,530/40, and clawed its way back up to $1,568, up $3 from Tuesday.
Traders said the market is not really responding to the string of inventory drawdowns, although there has not been heavy selling pressure.
On Thursday, the IPAI releases producer inventory data for May, but this is expected to have little impact, they said.
Lead and zinc both flipped back up into the plus column, closing at $650 and $1,462, up $1 and $3 respectively.

"Zinc has the best fundamentals, and has had a correction...lead should do well later in the third quarter, so there could be some pre-emptive buying ahead of the battery season," analyst Angus MacMillan of LME trader Billiton Metals said.
But tin and nickel lost ground. Tin closed $30 lower at $5,510, and is now seen re-testing 2-1/4 year lows of $5,490.

Nickel was only partially cushioned by the Falconbridge strike vote ahead of the labour contract expiry later this month. It finished $45 easier at $6,890, reflecting rising stocks and talk of ample Russian availability.
Alloy was marked down, and closed some $12 easier at $1,415/20 a tonne. --Martin Hayes, London Newsroom 44 171 542 8080
